---
title: "Do gut bacteria listen to stress hormones?"
description: "Norepinephrine is a human stress signal. Some bacteria also grow faster when it is around. That is a two-way street rarely discussed."
author: "Yannick Loth"
date: "2026-11-01"
categories: [Cross-links, Noradrenergic, Mechanisms]
---

Most gut-brain discussions run through the immune system. There is a second, stranger channel: **microbial endocrinology** — the study of how host hormones and neurotransmitters influence microbes, and vice versa.

The evidence is real but early. Norepinephrine increased the growth and virulence of at least one pathogenic bacterium, altering the expression of many virulence genes (@Gao2019NEAeromonas). And gut bacteria both produce and consume mammalian neurotransmitters, including norepinephrine (@Dicks2022GutBacteriaNeurotransmitters).

**Why it might matter for ME/CFS.** If host norepinephrine availability is altered — as the selective-deficit hypothesis suggests — it could change the local environment the gut microbiome sees, shifting the ecosystem. That would be a *host-to-microbe* effect, distinct from the usual microbe-to-immune-to-brain direction.

**The honest caveats.** The bacterial study used a fish pathogen, not a human gut organism. The reviews describe plausibility, not a demonstrated ME/CFS mechanism. And the core norepinephrine finding is unreplicated.

**How to test it.** Expose bacteria cultured from ME/CFS and control gut communities to norepinephrine and ask whether growth or virulence changes, and whether a patient's noradrenergic tone correlates with their microbiome composition. If not, the channel is interesting but not operative here.
